name: Charles's Law
statement: At constant pressure, a gas expands in step with its absolute temperature.
statementAccent: in step with its absolute temperature
meaning: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed amount of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. Heat the gas and it expands; cool it and it contracts, the volume tracking the temperature measured on the Kelvin scale. Divide volume by absolute temperature and the ratio stays fixed as long as the pressure holds.
mechanism: Absolute temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules. Heating speeds them up, so they strike the container walls harder and more often. To keep the pressure constant, the gas must expand, spreading the molecules out until the rate of collisions per unit area falls back to where it was. The result is that volume rises in direct proportion to absolute temperature. Extrapolating the straight line of volume against temperature backward, the volume would vanish at about minus 273 degrees Celsius: the origin of the absolute scale.

examples.text: Heating the air in a balloon expands it, making it less dense than the surrounding air so the balloon rises: the effect Charles, himself a pioneering balloonist, knew well.
Take an inflated balloon out into winter air or put it in a freezer and it visibly shrinks as the gas inside cools.
Extending the volume-temperature line down toward zero volume points to minus 273 degrees Celsius, a limit that helped establish the absolute temperature scale.

variants.name: The ideal gas law
variants.text: Charles's law is the special case of the ideal gas law with pressure and amount held fixed, one of the family that also includes Boyle's, Gay-Lussac's, and Avogadro's laws.

variants.name: The absolute-zero extrapolation
variants.text: The backward extension of the volume-temperature line to zero volume, historically important in fixing minus 273 degrees Celsius as absolute zero, though the gas condenses long before.

whyItMatters: It is one of the classic gas laws, capturing how gases swell with heat, and a building block of the ideal gas law that combines the lot. Its extrapolation to zero volume gave one of the first routes to the concept of absolute zero and the Kelvin scale, and its everyday consequences, from balloons to thermometers, make it a staple of introductory science.

working.text: always use absolute temperature; the proportionality holds only on the Kelvin scale, so convert from Celsius first.
apply the law only where the pressure and amount of gas stay fixed, letting volume and temperature vary together.
trust it at ordinary conditions but expect real gases to depart as they approach condensation.

limits: The law is an ideal-gas idealisation, best obeyed at low pressure and high temperature. It fails at low temperatures near a gas's condensation point, where the straight volume-temperature line breaks down, and at high pressures, where intermolecular forces and the finite volume of molecules cause deviations. It demands absolute temperature: the proportionality holds on the Kelvin scale, not in Celsius or Fahrenheit. And the extrapolation to zero volume is exactly that: an extrapolation, since real gases liquefy well before absolute zero.
misreadings: The volume is proportional to absolute temperature, not to the Celsius reading; heating a gas from ten to twenty degrees Celsius does not double its volume, because that is a rise of only a few per cent on the Kelvin scale. And the volume does not literally reach zero at minus 273 degrees Celsius: the gas condenses first, so that point is an extrapolated limit rather than an observed state.
origin: Formulated in unpublished work by Jacques Charles around 1787 and published by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac in 1802, who credited Charles; John Dalton independently studied the thermal expansion of gases around 1801. It is a special case of the ideal gas law.
